summary:
Nariño department stands under Colombia's national framework, which is among the most developed in Latin America on legal gender recognition. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official who defended the change described those examinations as profoundly invasive of privacy rights and rooted in unacceptable prejudice. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition, without a surgical requirement, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

The framework sits alongside lethal violence. Thirteen trans people were killed in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025, the Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, and more than 40 trans women were killed in 2023. Eight trans women were killed between February and April 2024. These figures are national and cover Nariño.

On 5 April 2025 a video went viral showing Sara Millerey, 32, attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia; she died of a second cardiac arrest at three the following afternoon, and no one had been arrested although police interrogated local residents. President Gustavo Petro asked authorities to investigate urgently, and events were held in several cities to denounce transphobia. Her mother Sandra Borja said: "They killed her for being who she was."

Some of the targeting is organised. In Caquetá, three armed men told trans woman Tatiana Cespedes, 51, she had one week to leave town or be killed; after hiding for a week she fled at night. "Social cleansing" flyers appeared on Caquetá streets and via WhatsApp naming "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets, a campaign by armed groups still operating despite the 2016 peace agreement. In Guajira, armed groups have posted flyers carrying a kill list of named individuals since March 2024. This armed-group violence, the threats and the resulting displacement are national in scope and cover Nariño.

Protection machinery exists but has not closed the gap. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, a crime against humanity. In May 2025 the UN Independent Expert on SOGI violence and discrimination, Graeme Reid, concluded a fact-finding mission across multiple Colombian cities, praising the government's legal reforms while warning of a stark disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience, with widespread discrimination and violence requiring urgent attention as killings rise.

Entry and partner recognition are settled in the visitor's favour. The first same-sex marriage conducted abroad was registered in Colombia in March 2016, and the National Registry issued a memo ordering all notaries and registrars to register same-sex marriages performed outside the country. Same-sex couples married abroad are entitled to the same visa, healthcare benefits, inheritance and pension rights as heterosexual spouses once they present a stamped marriage certificate and identification papers at the nearest designated office. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

Access to facilities and detention are covered by court order and administrative decree. Judgments T-314 of 2011 (Tequendama Hotel), T-909 of 2011 (Cosmocentro mall guards in Cali) and T-301 of 2004 (Santa Marta police at the city boardwalk) protect entry to public and commercial premises. A 2011 Constitutional Court ruling allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a Colombian court has since issued a ruling on the treatment of trans detainees.
tangentialFactors:
The violence recorded nationally is trans-specific rather than general crime: victims have been lured through a dating app and killed, a trans rough-sleeper was stabbed while sleeping, and others were killed in their homes or in a hairdresser. Reporting on the Millerey case describes calculated brutality persisting amid the country's decades-long civil conflict.

Economic marginalisation compounds the risk. Discrimination limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work, and in Caquetá trans women have few options beyond sex work, which concentrates exposure to armed groups and to the "social cleansing" campaigns those groups run.

The armed groups responsible for the flyer campaigns remained active more than eight years after the 2016 peace agreement, and the kill-list and cleansing notices circulate both as physical flyers and through WhatsApp, so the threat reaches a person before any physical encounter.

Colombia's trajectory is frequently used as a regional comparison point: formal legal protections are advanced, while international monitors record rising killings, a pattern the UN Independent Expert described as a disconnect between institutional progress and daily lived experience.
localsOnly:
Colombians change the sex marker on identification by signing a document before a notary, a route available since June 2015; bodily inspections and psychiatric assessments ordered by judges are no longer required, and no surgical condition applies.

The 2016 Ministry of Interior decree set procedural obligations for government institutions covering LGBTI rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and a May 2018 executive decree by President Juan Manuel Santos extended guarantees to housing, work, recreation, sports and culture.

Residents deprived of liberty have rulings in their favour: a 2011 Constitutional Court decision allowed a transgender woman prisoner to choose her own hairstyle and makeup, and a court has since ruled on the treatment of trans detainees.

People harmed in the conflict can seek recognition through the Special Jurisdiction for Peace, which in July 2023 charged 15 former rebels with war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, the state accepting that conflict-driven violence constituted gender persecution.

Same-sex couples have been able to marry since 2016 and to adopt since 2015, and the National Registry is under a standing instruction to register marriages performed abroad.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Nariño-specific departmental statistics on killings of trans people, on hate-crime charges, or on the number of marker changes processed in the department were located in the source inventory; the counts cited are national and the source states they cover Nariño, but a department-level breakdown is not sourced.

Whether the comprehensive trans law under legislative consideration in 2025 has since been enacted is unresolved in the sources.

Enforcement of the notary route and of the facility-entry judgments within Nariño specifically is not sourced; the obligations are national and their practical application in this department is unverified.

Whether armed-group kill-list or "social cleansing" flyer campaigns have been documented inside Nariño itself is not sourced; the inventory records them in Caquetá and Guajira and treats the threat as national.
